hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When a painful cancerous growth spread through Peregrine’s right leg, doctors scheduled an urgent amputation for the next morning. Next morning the stunned surgeon unwrapped the bandages to find completely healthy skin and bone! Peregrine lived twenty more years until age eighty.

detectiveClues.headline: "Come and See!" at Bethsaida on Galilee

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Aelium Cetium / Cannabiaca to uncover 3 hidden memories

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Firehouses across Europe, North America, and Australia proudly display St. Florian’s iconic Maltese cross badge on helmets, trucks, and station walls!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Every May 4 is celebrated worldwide as **International Firefighters’ Day** directly in honor of St. Florian’s feast day!
stops.saintQuote: Stand ready to rush in where others flee, trusting your life to God.

stops.imageCaption: Wide rushing silver-blue Alpine river beneath a sunlit medieval stone bridge framed by green Upper Austrian hills.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: After Florian’s body washed safely onto a river rock, a pious local woman named Valeria discovered him and gave him a reverent burial in the quiet countryside nearby!

completionSummary: You ran across the bustling playground of Turin with St. Dominic Savio—the cheerful fourteen-year-old student of St. John Bosco who stepped between stone-throwing schoolyard bullies, started the Immaculate Conception club, and proved holiness means being "always cheerful."

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Dominic’s modest family home in Morialdo and parish church in Riva welcome thousands of young pilgrims and altar servers every spring.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: At just fourteen years old when he died, St. Dominic Savio is the youngest non-martyr canonized in Catholic history—proving teenagers don’t have to wait until adulthood to live heroically!
stops.saintQuote: Here at Valdocco, we make holiness consist in being always cheerful!

detectiveClues.headline: Historical Footprint
detectiveClues.clueText: At just fourteen years old when he died, St. Dominic Savio is the youngest non-martyr canonized in Catholic history—proving teenagers don’t have to wait until adulthood to live heroically!

detectiveClues.headline: Four Promises at First Communion in Riva
detectiveClues.clueText: Born the son of a village blacksmith in Riva presso Chieri, energetic seven-year-old Dominic wrote four simple, joyful promises on the day of his First Communion: frequent Confession and Communion, keeping Sundays joyful, making Jesus and Mary his best friends, and "Death rather than sin!" Walking miles daily to school in scorching sun or winter snow, he met Fr. John Bosco at age twelve—and asked him, "Will you help make a fine suit for God out of my cloth?"

stops.title: Opening Italy’s First Free Girls’ School in Viterbo
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Viterbo to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden volcanic-stone medieval Italian piazza with arched doorways where smiling young women gather eagerly with slate boards and books.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Viterbo’s charming medieval streets preserve St. Rose Venerini’s birthplace and first schoolhouse as a proud milestone of women’s education.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Long before universal public schooling existed anywhere in Europe, Rose Venerini declared that educating women lifts up entire families and societies!
stops.saintQuote: Educate to free—for an enlightened mind and a loving heart transform the world.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Opening Italy’s First Free Girls’ School in Viterbo
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Born daughter of a respected physician in Viterbo, vibrant young Rose saw that poor girls were denied basic literacy and dignity while boys attended academies. Beginning simply by inviting neighborhood women to pray the Rosary in her living room, she opened Italy’s very first free public school for girls on August 30, 1685—facing mockery at first until the whole town marveled at how bright and confident her students grew!

stops.eraLabel: May 1630 · Banks of the Luján River

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Oxcart Miracle & Faithful "Negro Manuel"
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Resting overnight by the Luján River, the travelers yoked their oxen next morning—yet the cart refused to budge an inch! Adding extra oxen didn’t help. Unloading crates one by one, the cart rolled effortlessly the moment the tiny Immaculate Conception box was lifted down—and froze again the second they put it back! Understanding Mary wished to stay right there among the poor rural folk of the Pampas, they entrusted her care to a deeply devout African enslaved man named Manuel Costa de los Ríos ("Negro Manuel"), who lovingly tended her humble mud-brick chapel for fifty-six years.

stops.title: Converted by Kindness in Esna’s Prison

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Pachomius wasn’t converted by a debate or sermon—he became a Christian purely because ordinary unnamed villagers showed kindness to lonely prisoners!
stops.saintQuote: Who are these people who love strangers they have never met? I wish to serve their God forever.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Forcibly conscripted into the Roman army at age twenty, young pagan Pachomius was locked overnight with terrified recruits inside a grim prison in Latopolis (Esna). Amazed, Pachomius asked who these people were; told they were Christians who served the unseen God by loving strangers, he vowed on the spot to serve that God for the rest of his life.

stops.title: Lifting the Golden "IHS" in Piazza del Campo
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Piazza del Campo to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Vast sweeping shell-shaped sunlit Siena brick plaza packed with smiling townsfolk gazing up at a friar holding a gleaming golden sun-burst plaque inscribed IHS.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Look up above the grand Palazzo Pubblico right in Siena’s Piazza del Campo—St. Bernardine’s huge gilded bronze sun-badge "IHS" still gleams brightly there six hundred years later!

stops.title: Forgiving His Executioners in Colotlán
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Colotlán Municipal Courtyard to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Golden sunlit Mexican colonial stone courtyard archway bathed in warm quiet morning light symbolizing fearless mercy and forgiveness.

Arrested alongside his young friend Fr. detectiveClues.headline: Martyr of the Seal of Confession on Charles Bridge

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Santuario di Nostra Signora di Misericordia to uncover 3 hidden memories

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Savona’s coastal hills and Rome’s calendar still celebrate May 24 as a day of liberation, gratitude, and quiet trust during dark times.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Australia also chose **Mary, Help of Christians** as its official national Patroness in 1844—honored every May 24 from Sydney’s St. Mary’s Cathedral to the Outback!
stops.saintQuote: When every earthly door seems bolted shut, trust Mary—she knows every quiet path home.

stops.imageCaption: Majestic golden-domed Italian Renaissance basilica crowned by a gleaming bronze statue gleaming brightly above Turin and distant snowy Alps.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Turin’s Basilica of Mary Help of Christians stands as the vibrant worldwide motherhouse of the Salesian family—housing the shrines of St. John Bosco, St. Mary Mazzarello, and St. Dominic Savio.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. John Bosco famously summed up every miracle of his life in one smiling four-word sentence: "She has done everything!"
stops.saintQuote: Trust in Mary, Help of Christians, and you will see what miracles truly are.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When St. John Bosco began building the grand Basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin for his hundreds of street boys, he had literally just 40 cents in his pocket! Handing the contractor those few tiny coins with a twinkle in his eye, he promised: "Don’t worry—Mary will pay the bills!" Brick by brick, unexpected gifts arrived until the glorious basilica opened debt-free in 1868.

completionSummary: You sat by candlelight beside the North Sea with St. Bede the Venerable—Doctor of the Church, "Father of English History," astronomer of ocean tides, and the gentle monk who popularized the "AD" (Anno Domini) calendar used worldwide today.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Wearmouth Abbey to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: c. 680 AD · Mouth of the River Wear
stops.imageCaption: Sturdy Anglo-Saxon golden sandstone church porch glowing beside North Sea coastal winds and tall sunlit grasses.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The original seventh-century Anglo-Saxon stone west porch and tower of St. Peter’s Church in Monkwearmouth STILL stand over 1,340 years later!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Bede is the ONLY native-born English saint ever declared a universal Doctor of the Church—and Dante placed him proudly in Paradise in the Divine Comedy!
stops.saintQuote: It has always been my delight to learn, or to teach, or to write.

trailSubtitle: 3 Stops · Liège Vision of St. Juliana, Basilica of Santa Cristina Bolsena & Orvieto Cathedral
globeHeaderSubtitle: Sacred Trails of Corpus Christi Trail (Liège, Bolsena & Orvieto Cathedral)
completionSummary: You traced the breathtaking origin of the Feast of Corpus Christi—from the moon-vision of young St. Juliana in Liège, Belgium to the 1263 Eucharistic Miracle of Bolsena and the shimmering mosaic cathedral crowning the volcanic cliff of Orvieto.

stops.title: St. Juliana’s Vision of the Full Moon in Liège
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mont-Cornillon, Liège to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Luminous silver-gold full moon glowing above medieval stone Belgian monastery roofs beside the tranquil Meuse River.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The historic Church of St. Martin in Liège still celebrates the world’s original Corpus Christi roots begun by humble St. Juliana.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Archdeacon Jacques Pantaléon of Liège—who personally listened to St. Juliana’s dream—later became Pope Urban IV and gave Corpus Christi to the entire world!
stops.saintQuote: How brightly shines the calendar when gratitude for Christ’s living presence crowns the year.

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in the quiet village of Domrémy-la-Pucelle (Vosges department in the Grand Est / Lorraine region of northeastern France), visitors walk inside Joan’s preserved 15th-century stone Birthplace House, touch her original baptismal font in the parish church of Saint-Rémy, and visit the hilltop Basilica of Bois-Chenu.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When King Charles VII ennobled Joan and her family in 1429, he exempted the village of Domrémy from all royal taxes in perpetuity. Every year in the royal tax ledger beside the name "Domrémy," French tax collectors simply wrote three words: "Néant, la Pucelle" ("Nothing—on account of the Maid")!
stops.saintQuote: “I was thirteen when I had a Voice from God to help me govern myself. And the first time, I was very much afraid.”

detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the Vosges department of northeastern France along the green valley of the Meuse River. In 1578, this village officially added "-la-Pucelle" ("The Maid") to its name in honor of its most famous daughter.

detectiveClues.headline: 360 Years of "Néant, la Pucelle" in the French Royal Tax Books!
detectiveClues.clueText: From 1429 until the French Revolution in 1789, residents of this village paid zero royal taxes—and Joan’s sloped-roof stone family cottage still stands intact beside the parish church where she was baptized!

detectiveClues.headline: The Midday Summer Light in Her Father’s Garden at Age 13 (1425)
detectiveClues.clueText: Born here around January 6, 1412 to farmer Jacques d’Arc and Isabelle Romée, 13-year-old Joan heard the voices of St. Michael the Archangel, St. Catherine, and St. Margaret calling her to lift the siege of Orléans.

stops.title: The Captain’s Sword & The Ride Through the Gate of France
stops.subtitle: Examine the medieval Porte de France and Castle Chapel in Vaucouleurs
stops.imageCaption: Fortified medieval stone Porte de France (Gate of France) and Castle Chapel in Vaucouleurs, Lorraine, France, where Joan rode out in February 1429.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Vaucouleurs (18 km north of Domrémy in the Meuse department of northeastern France), visitors walk beneath the original 14th-century stone archway of the Porte de France, descend into the Castle Chapel crypt to see the 14th-century statue of Our Lady of the Vaults, and view the ancient linden tree where Joan tied her horse.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Garrison commander Robert de Baudricourt twice laughed 17-year-old Joan out of Vaucouleurs, telling her uncle to "take her home and box her ears." Only on her third visit—when she accurately announced the French defeat at the Battle of the Herrings before any courier could arrive—did he hand her a sword and say: "Go, and come what may!"
stops.saintQuote: “Even if I had to crawl on my knees, I would go to the Dauphin, for there is no one else in the world who can recover the Kingdom of France.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #2 · The Garrison Gate Where the Skeptical Captain Handed Her a Sword
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then locate the loyal Meuse garrison town just north of Domrémy where Captain Robert de Baudricourt equipped Joan for her ride.

detectiveClues.headline: A Hilltop Garrison Town in the Meuse Department, 18 km North of Domrémy
detectiveClues.clueText: Look just 18 km north down the Meuse River from Domrémy in northeastern France. On its castle hill still stands the medieval stone archway called the "Porte de France" (Gate of France).

detectiveClues.headline: "Go, and Come What May!" & The Townspeople Who Bought Her a Horse
detectiveClues.clueText: Once gruff Captain Robert de Baudricourt finally relented here in February 1429, the townspeople pooled 16 francs to buy 17-year-old Joan a horse and riding tunic, while Baudricourt buckled a sword to her side!

detectiveClues.headline: Riding Out with Six Escorts on the Evening of February 23, 1429
detectiveClues.clueText: After praying in the subterranean crypt of Our Lady of the Vaults, Joan rode out through the Porte de France at dusk on February 23, 1429 with six armed companions on an 11-day dash across 300 miles of enemy territory.

stops.title: The Disguised Dauphin & The Great Hall on the Vienne
stops.subtitle: Survey the Royal Fortress of Chinon above the Vienne River in the Loire Valley
stops.imageCaption: Royal Fortress of Chinon perched on the limestone bluff above the Vienne River in the Loire Valley, France.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Chinon (Indre-et-Loire in the Loire Valley of central-western France, 45 km southwest of Tours), visitors ascend the cliff-top Royal Fortress of Chinon, pass beneath the 14th-century Clock Tower housing the Joan of Arc Museum, and stand beside the preserved stone fireplace wall of the Great Hall where Joan recognized the Dauphin.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: To test whether 17-year-old Joan was truly sent by God, Dauphin Charles dressed a courtier in royal robes on the throne while he hid plainly dressed among 300 nobles in the torchlit Great Hall of Chinon. Joan walked straight past the decoy throne and knelt before the real Dauphin!
stops.saintQuote: “Gentle Dauphin, my name is Joan the Maid; the King of Heaven sends you word through me that you shall be anointed and crowned in the city of Reims.”

detectiveClues.headline: The Torchlit Decoy Throne Test & The Secret Sign Whispered to the Prince
detectiveClues.clueText: In the Great Hall here on the evening of March 8, 1429, surrounded by 50 torches and 300 courtiers, Joan bypassed a richly dressed decoy on the throne, went straight to the disguised Dauphin Charles, and whispered a secret prayer only he knew!

detectiveClues.headline: Housed in the Tower of Coudray & The Sword of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois
detectiveClues.clueText: After an 11-day ride from Vaucouleurs, Joan lodged in the keep of Coudray inside this fortress and directed messengers to unearth an ancient sword with five crosses buried behind the altar of nearby Fierbois.

stops.eraLabel: April 29 – May 8, 1429 AD · The Maid of Orléans
stops.imageCaption: Twin-towered Gothic Cathedral of Sainte-Croix and the bronze equestrian statue of St. Joan of Arc in Orléans, France.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Orléans (on the northern bend of the Loire River, 120 km south of Paris, France), visitors marvel at the stained-glass windows of Sainte-Croix Cathedral depicting Joan’s life, visit the Maison de Jeanne d’Arc (the half-timbered house of treasurer Jacques Boucher where she stayed), and stand in Place du Martroi.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Although a seven-month siege had brought Orléans to the brink of surrender, 17-year-old Joan lifted the entire siege in just nine days (April 29 – May 8, 1429)! At her trial she explained why she carried her white linen banner into battle: "I loved my banner forty times better than my sword, so that I would never kill anyone!"
stops.saintQuote: “In God’s name, let us go on boldly! Enter among them—all is yours!”

stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to the strategic Loire River city whose seven-month siege Joan broke in May 1429.

detectiveClues.headline: Capital of the Centre-Val de Loire Region at the Northernmost Bend of the Loire
detectiveClues.clueText: Look 120 km south of Paris where the mighty Loire River curves farthest north. Because of her victory here in May 1429, Joan is universally known as the "Maid of [This City]."

detectiveClues.headline: Europe’s Oldest Civic Festival Celebrated Every May 8 Since 1429!
detectiveClues.clueText: Every single year since May 8, 1429—for nearly 600 years—this city has celebrated the Fêtes Johanniques, choosing a local high-school girl to ride in full armor to Sainte-Croix Cathedral!

detectiveClues.headline: Storming the Tourelles Fortress & Praying at Sainte-Croix (May 1429)
detectiveClues.clueText: Entering the besieged city by boat at night with supply wagons on April 29, 1429, Joan rallied the defenders—even after taking an arrow above her collarbone at the Tourelles—and broke the siege in nine days.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Carrying her white linen banner inscribed "Jhesus Maria," 17-year-old Joan entered besieged Orléans on April 29, 1429. On May 7, despite being wounded by a crossbow bolt between her neck and shoulder, she returned to the ditch at sunset to lead the final charge that captured the Tourelles fortress, ending the siege the next morning!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: On the evening of May 2 and again after victory on May 8, 1429, Joan attended solemn thanksgiving prayers inside Sainte-Croix Cathedral while citizens crowded around to touch her white banner—which she carried in hand so she would never strike down any person with a sword!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Reims (130 km northeast of Paris in the Champagne region of France), visitors enter the UNESCO Gothic masterpiece of Notre-Dame de Reims Cathedral—where 33 French kings were crowned—to stand on the choir stones where Joan wept with joy beside newly anointed King Charles VII on July 17, 1429.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When asked after the five-hour coronation ceremony in Reims Cathedral why her white banner had been given the place of honor right beside the King at the altar, Joan gave one of the most famous replies in history: "It had borne the burden; it earned the honor!" stops.saintQuote: “Gentle King, now is fulfilled the pleasure of God, who willed that I should lift the siege of Orléans and bring you to this city of Reims to receive your holy coronation!”

detectiveClues.headline: Fulfilling the Prophecy of Chinon on Sunday, July 17, 1429

stops.title: The Cross Held High & The Rehabilitation of the Maid
stops.subtitle: Explore the Place du Vieux-Marché and Memorial Cross in Rouen
stops.imageCaption: Tall stone Memorial Cross and the boat-roofed Church of Sainte-Jeanne-d’Arc in the half-timbered Place du Vieux-Marché in Rouen, Normandy, France.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Rouen (capital of Normandy on the lower Seine River in northwestern France), visitors stand in the medieval half-timbered Place du Vieux-Marché beside the 20-meter National Memorial Cross, enter the sweeping Church of Sainte-Jeanne-d’Arc, and visit the Archbishop’s Palace ("Historial Jeanne d’Arc") where her 1456 Nullification Trial declared her innocent.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Every single word 19-year-old Joan spoke during her 1431 trial in Rouen was recorded verbatim by three court notaries—making Joan of Arc the most thoroughly documented person of the entire Middle Ages! Twenty-five years later in the same Archbishop’s Palace in Rouen (July 7, 1456), 115 witnesses testified and the Inquisitor General solemnly annulled her conviction!
stops.saintQuote: “Hold the cross high so that I may see it through the flames! … Jesus, Jesus!”

stops.title: Two Mothers Embracing at the Church of the Visitation
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Summer House of Zechariah & Elizabeth to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden Mediterranean hillside stone courtyard lined with olive trees where a young woman and her joyful silver-haired cousin embrace warmly.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside Ein Karem’s lovely two-story Church of the Visitation, serene frescoes and multilingual ceramic plaques celebrate the first meeting of Jesus and John the Baptist.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Every single evening at Vespers (Evening Prayer) across monasteries and parishes worldwide, Christians sing Mary’s Visitation hymn—the Magnificat!
stops.saintQuote: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Summer House of Zechariah & Elizabeth in the scene.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Two Mothers Embracing at the Church of the Visitation
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: The very instant Mary’s warm greeting echoed across Elizabeth’s threshold, six-month-old unborn John the Baptist leaped with joy inside Elizabeth’s womb! Filled with the Holy Spirit, Elizabeth cried the immortal words still prayed in every Hail Mary: "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!"—and Mary answered with the joyful song of the Magnificat.

stops.title: Three Months of Humble Service & Birth of John

stops.eraLabel: c. 6 – 5 BC · Church of St. John in the Mountains
stops.imageCaption: Peaceful whitewashed stone Judean village terrace overlooking terraced olive valleys glowing amber as neighbors celebrate a newborn child.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Just across the fragrant valley from the Visitation shrine stands the Franciscan Church of St. John the Baptist, where pilgrims read Zechariah’s "Benedictus" hymn tiled in dozens of languages.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: The Visitation is the Second Joyful Mystery of the Rosary—and Christians pray it whenever asking for the grace of "love of neighbor"!
stops.saintQuote: He has lifted up the lowly and filled the hungry with good things.
